You are an expert Legal AI performing a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) compliance audit.
Target Data Subject: Michael Burke
Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michel, Michael B., M. Burke

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newest messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.
4. "DISCARD" DECISION (THREAD DECAY): You MUST return "discard" if the Data Subject's only appearance is deep in a large email chain (e.g. message 3, 4, 5+ in the thread history) and they are no longer an active participant in the recent correspondence.
5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. IGNORE TECHNICAL DATABASE METADATA: The JSON payload contains tracking properties such as "emailHash", "parentHash", and "sequentialName". These are administrative tracking keys used strictly for folder organization and deduplication logic. You MUST ignore these keys completely. Do NOT use them, their values, or their presence to influence your audit decisions. Base your review strictly on actual communication properties: "from", "to", "subject", "date", and "body".
7. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

{"emailHash":"537aaa668fbac8e10d2dd61fca03f223746af617951367ee68ad03738ab4eb3e","parentHash":null,"from":"Anna Varga","to":"Plate Litigation; Alicia Alinia; Raminder Grewal","subject":"Fw: Wish List & Requests","date":"2025-10-09T17:26:09.000Z","attachments":true,"body":"


 P {margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;} 



Raminder




If that call with Charlie goes ahead this will be of relevance - I've not considered fully - but the point of this email was to provide some items we could put to LD re continued involvement.




Have we reminded the team and more broadly about the employee assistance programme?

A
​​​​Anna VargaPartner+44 (0) 7890 043 699

From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Thursday, October 9, 2025 6:13 PM
To: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>
Cc: Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Sarah Bingham <sbingham@pogustgoodhead.com>; Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Wish List & Requests
 






Hi Anna,




Following on from yesterday and the calls with LD, a few things we would suggest are raised with Martyn. Firstly, it is important to say the Case Leads and PG team are wildly committed to this trial. That should not be in question.
 However, the AA (the executed version of which the case leads were only sent at 9.22AM this morning), which has been referred to in Court documents and has been incepted without the consent of those persons it applies to (either expressly in the case of the
 Case Leads or, as far as the wider team is concerned, by implication), causes concern. Additionally, the case leads have also raised serious concerns about the staff's  mental health that are yet to be addressed by the firm.




The AA was incepted with little to no visibility or consideration for how it will practically work (as is clear given Martyn's explanation in ​the call on 8 October was substantially different to our understanding of what it means,
 a view which we consider you, also on that call, shared). We need further clarity on the AA. This is true for both for the Case Leads, and the PG staff who will be indirectly subject to it - by way of taking instructions from the Case Leads who are under the
 supervision of Leigh Day.  As we have already told you, there is a real risk of the substantive PG team being entirely alienated by this agreement. These concerns were evidently ignored (including our concerns over the mental health and well-being of the staff)
 given it was executed without further recourse to us.  It also remains unclear what, if any, interaction LD is to have with the wider PG team, if they are not subject to the AA (and therefore direction and supervision), and whether, given this, the PG team
 would need to revert to one of the Case Leads for every interaction, instruction, discussion had with the LD team. An obvious example of this is the trial bundle/logistics workstreams which have largely been left between the excellent PG associates and LD
 with limited input from the case leads. It is fair to say the PG team carries that workstream and LD are unprepared to take it on. Similarly with Opus and issues at this morning's hearing. 




It would be helpful for an explanation, and for the physical AA, to be sent out to the wider PG team along with some practical guidance about what it means. It would be inappropriate for the Case Leads to do this given: i) we
 haven’t agreed to the AA; and ii) it has been incepted against our consent.




It would be helpful if the explanation covered:





what LD expect from the PG team  - do they simply expect the PG teams to "do what they're told, when they're told", or is there still going to be a collaborative
 approach (the former seems more likely given how things have happened over the last few days); 


how the "do what they're told, when they're told" works - or, indeed wider interaction works, in circumstances where the team isn't caught by the agreement. Will they need to take each instruction and run it past a Case Lead?

what happens in circumstances where the PG teams disagree with LDs position on decisions? How does this get resolved between the firms? We stress this is not a hypothetical. Aside from wider case strategy
 we have had immediate differences in opinion last week in terms of costs, with decisions being made and taken without reference to PG. This impacts all claimants, and, of course PG's clients. Further, in terms of wider points, as we have pointed out, LD do
 not have clients on some of the secondary or ALGLO cases, all of which are bound by the PDD trial judgment. It is easy to anticipate a diversion of opinion/strategy as the PDD trial develops which could impact PG only cases/clients and for which, under the
 AA the Case Leads cannot wear two hats.  

how working practices are going to change, both outwardly to the Ds and Court etc, and whether a working group should be set up to standardise approach e.g. do all things on the PG SharePoint move across
 to LD - what is the timeframe, how is it co-ordinated? Whilst an administrative concern this does have significance in terms of sheer volume and also maintaining/transferring admin rights for links particularly where the Defendants and the Court already retain
 access. 

How does it work for the costs team? 





Each of these, along with sight of the AA, will go some way to helping the PG staff understand the agreement they are now working under and hopefully to stop the wheels from falling off. This will also assist in answering questions
 the Case Leads have, but it will not, we doubt, satisfy any regulatory concerns we have, and we request again the Board's complete answer to our note of 05.10.2025 (under cover of email of Sarah Bingham). To date we have not had any answer from you. 




On this point, we thought it helpful to also compile a few outstanding requests from our end to you / the Board. We should also say thank you again for speaking to Alicia and arranging the call with the employment solicitor. While
 we hope this will assist in clarifying the position in terms of whether this AA can be imposed upon us and not contravene our employment contracts, it will not be able to answer any of our regulatory concerns (in respect of the AA and wider regulatory concerns).
 These really can only be answered by the following: 





the advice from BWKC or any other counsel on the AA. This is especially true where many of the concerns we have raised overlap with those in the HSFK letter - including the regulatory position for us
 as lawyers, and the position on client consent. We still have not consented to the AA and we all have significant regulatory concerns. In particular we have not seen any advice which contradicts our position that client consent is necessary for the AA.

Re the AA and how strategic decisions are made, a very practical question: in circumstances where LD and PG (either collaboratively or by PG being informed)
 make a decision, do the PG bods have to in turn report these to the Board / AV? Do we have to report where decisions have been made that we do not agree with? What is our internal reporting matrix for issues such as this? 

Will our COLP, in their role as COLP, be giving us sign off on the agreement, in addition to the Counsel advice?

As our COLP is now also a case lead (for Pan NOx and it appears individual cases), is there a delineation of the COLP roles, from the role of case lead,
 and CEO of the firm? How is this safeguarded?





If these questions are not answered to a satisfactory standard, then our regulatory concerns will remain and as regulated persons, we will need to consider our positions and what, if any, further steps we need to take.




Thanks,




Case Leads
































​​​​




























Michael Burke









(He/Him)















Partner











+44 (0) 7960 032 344















07960 032 344































"}

This is such a disappointing and self-serving message. For young lawyers who have little experience of the ups and downs of life, he's made this very procedural change sound utterly earth shattering. Sent from Outlook for iOS​​​​Alicia AliniaChief Executive Officer+44 (0) 7890 043 629From: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Friday, October 10, 2025 6:57 amTo: Plate Litigation <plate_litigation@pallasllp.com>; Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Fw: Looking Ford-ward Sent from Outlook for iOS​​​​Anna VargaPartner+44 (0) 7890 043 699From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Thursday, October 9, 2025 10:57:47 PMTo: Ford Litigation Team <fordteam@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Looking Ford-ward Team,Over the last few days post the Lead Solicitor application, I and the other case leads, have been engaging with LD to establish what our brave new world will look like and how the teams implement it. Ultimately, whether we like it or not (and barring the Court going completely left field in their judgment tomorrow), LD are going to be the sole Lead Solicitor on the Ford Litigation. I am genuinely sorry that this has happened and that things have happened the way that they have. None of you deserve to the subject to this. This juncture has been reached through no fault of any of yours and believe me when I say I know just how unpleasant it feels. I also fully appreciate that it sucks even more to know that, despite how much it feels like we've been relegated to "just another claimant firm", we will still need to perform largely the same role that we have been before now - except we do it without the title of Lead Solicitor.  As we try to gather some understanding of how this new world will practically work, especially with the Agency Agreement that the firms have executed, there are a few things that look to have been decided that I can inform you of:The AA (as the firms have executed) puts me under the supervision of LD - it does not extend to you as individuals. You will still work under PG and your day jobs go on as normal. How this works for me and my instructions to you, we are all trying to get to the bottom of. You are all smart lawyers and I am sure you can appreciate that I may have some concerns over how this works in practice, but I (and the other case leads) will be doing what we can to a) ensure you are fully equipped and supported to do you job and b) find a solution that works for everyone so we can move forward;LD will take over all comms (incoming and outgoing) to the Ds. As part of the AA that the firms have agreed, I will be CC'ed on those emails, and I will then need to pass them onto the team along with instructions;Similar with external meetings with the Defendants. The de facto is that LD will attend these solo but there will inevitably be instances where PG team members are needed;Communications with counsel etc can (I believe) proceed as normal and we shouldn't have to run these past LD, but if that changes, I will let you know;All external work on the PG SharePoint that is "common work" will at some stage be moved over to the LD SharePoint - this is to ensure links going out to the Ds etc go from a Leigh Day email account (the timeline on this is very much TBC becuase of how big of a task it is);Group Register (and Notice of Objection) work has not yet been decided but §19 of the Ford GLO dictates that PG have responsibility for this, not the Lead Solicitor, so it is likely that this will remain as it has been. I will update on this when I know more;Trial preparation and attendance is expected to be as it would have been otherwise. I have been today working on a rota for who will be where, when. Executive Summary

Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's

 cross-examination was quite short.

Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.

 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of

Week 3 and 4: Mercedes




Following the previous updates, please see below update regarding the Mercedes portion of the trial which ran from 29 October until 6 November. 




There is significant correlation between Ford and Mercedes, as indeed there is across each of the 5 lead manufacturers, in that the technology that each manufacturer used is broadly similar i.e. they all used one of, or a combination of, the following types
 of technology; exhaust gas re-circulation ("EGR"), Lean NOx Traps ("LNT"), selective catalytic reduction ("SCR") and diesel particular filter ("DPF"). Each manufacturer used these technologies and strategies to varying degrees and
 in different ways with different calibrations and to differing levels of success. This in itself is helpful for our claim as their arguments and the reality of how they used the technology variously cut across each other as to the component limits or availability
 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way. 

Since Mercedes did not call factual witnesses, the examinations concerned expert evidence only. This, in our opinion and in our submissions to the Court, is quite illuminating.


Claimants’ Expert: 



Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation. 


 

Week 4: Mercedes Software and Mechanical Engineering Evidence (3-6 November)  

Week four saw further cross-examination of the Claimants' experts, Dr Heitz (software engineering who is the same expert in Mercedes and Ford, as he is for all of the cases for the Claimants) and Mr Smithers and of the Defendants’ expert witnesses, Dr John
 Martens (software engineering) and Raoul Spencer Day (mechanical engineering).

The Claimants' counsel team focused on the internal engineering and software design choices within Mercedes-Benz vehicles, arguing these revealed deliberate calibration to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world compliance. The Defendants’ experts
 on the other hand maintained that the systems reflected legitimate engineering trade-offs, a similar argument to that which For dare attempting to advance.    

Claimants’ Experts: 



Dr Heitz and Mr Smithers confirmed that Mercedes’ SCR system used different dosing modes in tests and in real driving conditions, with higher AdBlue dosing — and therefore lower NOx — only under test conditions.   


The Claimants' experts’ position was that Mercedes’ firmware and calibration choices aligned with test-cycle boundaries (notably the NEDC 20–30°C temperature range) and that NOx emissions rose sharply just outside these parameters. This confirmed “cycle recognition”
 behaviour. 


Defendants’ Experts: 



Dr John Martens & Raoul Spencer Day (Ricardo plc) were challenged over their objectivity as experts in this litigation, given their extensive work for car manufacturers and commercial ties to several Defendants. They confirmed such relationships.   


Mr Day accepted that Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (“PEMS”) could have been used to calibrate vehicles for real-world driving but were not, and conceded that Mercedes’ firmware initially switched off NOx controls at altitude — this was later
 corrected by software updates.  


He accepted that US models used more effective emission hardware, with EU models prioritising fuel economy instead. This is positive for Ford given this is a tenet of our allegations against Ford.



Mercedes insisted these differences reflected regional regulations and safety trade-offs, not cheating, and claimed the Emissions Regulation applied mainly to type-approval tests rather than real-world conditions.

Dear all,




I hope you are well and are enjoying the half term break. 




I write in relation three matters, one of which we require your instructions in relation to:





an update on the second week of trial;

an application by the Ford Defendants to amend some of their pleadings -
we require your instructions in relation to this; and

the discontinuance of Mr Gormley (as previously discussed in my update of 26 September 2025.





Second and third week of trial




Week two of the PDD Trial focused on the issue of what are conditions which are “reasonably likely to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use” for the purposes of identifying prohibited defeat devices in the Defendants’ vehicles. The Court
 heard from experts in the field of what constitutes "normal driving" and climatology. For the Claimants, our experts were Professor Tate (normal driving) and Professor Mills (climatology) and for the Defendants, Professor Hausberger (normal driving) and Professor
 Chapman (climatology). 




Ultimately, while this was important evidence which will underpin the definition of "prohibited defeat device", as the Judge remarked at the end of the evidence - it would not be a central part of her ultimate judgment. 




That said, and as we have advised our insurers; we think that the Claimants’ evidence and cross-examination of the Defendants’ experts has clearly had a positive impact on the judge’s views of this element of the case. While we anticipate that the likely approach
 Lady Justice Cockerill will take is to set a limit on the range of conditions which would reasonably be encountered during normal vehicle operation and use, however, we do not expect that she will be inclined to adopt an excessively restrictive set of boundaries
 (which the Defendants have advocated for) in light of the Claimants’ case on this issue.




Starting tomorrow, Mercedes kicks us off into the manufacturer specific sections of the trial. Mercedes will run from tomorrow, 29 October 2025, until 6 November. Ford then starts on 10 November and runs until 18 November. Preparations for Ford are going well.
 As previously offered, if any of you wish to attend on the 10,11,12,13, 17 or 18 November, please let me know. You are most welcome to attend and we can arrange for this to happen. 




Defendants' application to amend




On Friday afternoon, we received correspondence from the Ford Defendants, proposing amendments to two of their Individual Defences. Their reason for this exceptionally late application, they have said, is that they have given "careful consideration to the
 fidelity of their pleadings in light of those [opening] submissions, and have taken the view that two of the IDEFS....out properly to be amended." The effect of these amendments is that they are seeking to change their case on a central point of dispute
 between the parties. As summarised by one of the Claimants legal team - these proposed amendments mean "at the very lease, their legal representatives (and their mechanical expert) were misled (though they would very likely say they were misinformed)". 




While we would be within our right to refuse these amendments, having taken advice from our counsel team, we are minded to permit the Defendants to have these amendments, on the proviso that they pay our costs on the indemnity basis. Costs on the indemnity
 basis in essence mean that becuase the conduct of the paying party has been unreasonable, the burden to prove that the costs claimed is less. In practical terms, it means that the costs recovered are generally higher than otherwise. Counsel have also
 advised that it is in our favour to permit this as it allows us to put under the Judge's nose that the Ds have in essence lied, or at least not been fully truthful, about the software in their vehicles. 




We have written to the Defendants to propose this, but ultimately we must also take your instructions on this. It is our advice that, in the event Ford agree to pay our wasted costs, we will consent to the application.
Can you please confirm by return that you instruct us to consent to the application?




Mr Gormley




As you may recall from my 26 September update and from the instructions you provided, you instructed us to take the following steps:





Proceed to discontinue Mr Gormley’s claim in England & Wales; and
Remove Mr Gormley from the Ford Group Register.

We are in the process of doing so. We have liaised with the ATE  provider on this as there are, as advised, necessarily costs associated with this. The insurers have confirmed that they will cost the costs of this discontinuance, but reserve the right to seek
 them from Pogust Goodhead or the client at the conclusion of the matter is so required. 




We will now proceed with the discontinuance of Mr Gormely's claim. No further action is required form you in respect of this. 




Summary




Please confirm your instructions to me on the Defendants' application to amend. 




I will endeavour to provide you with an update in advance of Ford being heard, however it may not be until the end of the Ford aspect of the trial that I am able to update you.




If you have any questions about any of this update, please let me know.




Kind regards,




Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Dear all,

I hope you are well.




I write to provide you with a brief update now we have concluded the opening week of the trial. 




Monday and Tuesday were for the Claimants to provide their opening submissions to the Court on the Lead Cases, while Wednesday and Thursday were and are for each of the Defendants to provide their response. Ford was covered across Monday and Tuesday morning
 by the Claimants, and then the Ford Defendants made their response on Wednesday.  




In relation to Ford - our take on the openings is that all of the Defendants were taken aback by how strongly we put the case to Ford. We do not think they expected for us to so aggressively put Ford at the front and centre in our opening and would have instead
 been prepared for us to instead turn our attention to some of the other Defendants. Our counsel team put on screen a number of extremely damaging documents, which various of the press and NGOs who were in attendance also took note of. These documents included
 internal emails between Ford employees where they discussed updates to improve the vehicles in circumstances where they were considered to be in the worse 20% of vehicles in the EU. Similarly, we also displayed Ford internal presentations showing how test
 results which were above regulatory limits, were in fact "in line with Ford's expectations". The Court looked interested in these documents




Ford's response we have opined was a little underwhelming, focusing on how Ford self-profess to be industry standard bearers for compliance and how the Claimants have not appropriately set out our case, while failing to deal with the more damaging information,
 something which we believe the Judge acutely noticed. We also ensured that our mechanical expert, Mr Carder, was in attendance yesterday so he is more familiar with the court layout in advance of his attendance for examination and cross examination. 




The summary is that there were no "rabbit out of a hat" reveals from any of the Defendants and the trial will roll onto next week with things having not markedly shifted this week.

Morning Sarah,
 
Ahead of our call to discuss at 11:30am, I just thought I’d flag some initial thoughts on the below, which we can then discuss later.
 
Wording of draft Order
Happy to discuss later this morning, but from my perspective, I’m not too concerned by Ds’ drafting of para 3.
For Experts, it seems to me inevitable that the court will want to budget them once the question of disciplines is resolved (and will want to whatever the wording of the order).
For ADR, wouldn’t it be in the Claimants’ favour
not to budget (given the scale of our estimates, and the likely approach which the court would take to them), if the court had any inclination not to do so? If so, don’t we want to give room for the court to decide that ADR is actually too difficult/uncertain
 to budget at the moment, rather than say they are forced to do so?
If that’s right, I would be inclined to go with Ds’ version of paragraph 3. But happy to discuss on our call.
 
CMH2 Consequentials
This has reminded me – have we had a decision on the CMH costs order yet?
 
Timing of CMH3 (Or CMH2.2, however we want to think of it!)
I agree that if there is to be further budgeting post-January we will need to crack on with it, there’s no point trying to drag our heels.
However, query whether a Feb CMH is a bit ambitious. Presumably we need time, post Jan CMC to:

Collect estimates based on decisions made, and update the 2x phases – min 10 days?Time for updates Prec Rs, in both directions – min 7 days?Gap to a hearing – c.7-10 days?
I can see that it wouldn’t be ideal to have the CMH in March, but I can see it happening as a matter of practicality, and it shouldn’t be the end of the world. It would be a fairly
 short and straightforward hearing.
I also doubt that it will really be possible to know exactly how much time will be required until at the Jan 26 CMC and hearing what the judges are deciding needs to be done.
Again, if the impracticalities end up pushing the court away from budgeting (at least in respect of ADR, which is likely to be harder than Experts), is that necessarily a bad thing?
(Also, surely the ADR costs wouldn’t start being incurred until end of April 2026, given they are in Second General?)
 
Whether costs counsel need to attend at the Jan CMC (22-23 Jan 2026)
Unfortunately(?) I am in Mexico from 17-31 Jan, but I will ask the clerks re Ben and Theo.
 
Budgeting framework
Unless it’s something the Ds are keen on, I’d be minded to just keep this as simple as possible. I don’t think this is a variation because there has been no budget set for Experts/ADR
 as phases.
I think the starting point, and probably the simplest answer, is that there would be two fresh phases for Experts and ADR with ‘incurred’ costs running (in the way we have done it
 previously) to the date of CMH3 – save that, for ADR, so long as the hearing was before the end of April, that would actually remain unchanged.
Once set, the ADR phase could be added to an updated Second General quite easily, as the incurred date is likely to be unaffected.
But even for the Experts, I don’t see why that couldn’t be added to the same document as the other T3 phases, once set. It would have a different ‘incurred’ cut off date, but everyone
 would know that (the relevant order would make it clear) and we could add a footnote to the face of the budget for the avoidance of doubt.
Overall, my view is we should (a) keep it simple, and (b) seek to agree our proposed approach with Ds in advance, much like we did on incurred dates previously. I don’t think we should
 decide our approach without knowing what their thoughts on it are.
 
Preparation for Budgeting
Let’s perhaps discuss this on the call.
It seems like there might be some discussions which can be had in advance of the Jan CMC in relation to different foreseeable scenarios to get the ball rolling on information gathering.
 But my first reaction is that these various potential changes, and the likelihood we won’t know which applies until 23 Jan, is why a February 2026 seems a little ambitious to me.
 
Other variations to T2/First General Budgets
I suppose it will depend on what the details of the envisaged variations are, but I am sceptical about whether the court will have any appetite for engaging in questions of variations
 to the T2/G1 budgets at this stage. Surely the costs will all have been incurred by the time any such variation hearing comes to be held (and perhaps even before we make an application)?
If that’s right, the court will surely say that these are questions to be dealt with on the basis of whether there is a ‘good reason to depart’ on assessment, rather than a variation
 (which is intended to be a largely prospective process). See Persimmon Homes Ltd & Anor v Osborne Clark & Anor
[2021] EWHC 831 (Ch), at [134]-[136].
And in any event, we would have to be conscious of the risk that:

The Ds use it as an opportunity to object and definitive close down any hope of recovering the additional costs (rather than leaving open the question of a
 ‘good reason to depart’); andDs might well say their costs have increased too, and seek their own increases to those budgets, with knock-on consequences for ATE levels etc.
 
Looking forward to discussing further at 11:30.

EXTERNAL EMAIL

Dear Ben, Theo and Simon,


We are writing in advance of the January 2026 CMC to flag the preparatory work required for the non-budgeted phases
 following CMH2.


Background and inconsistency in draft order
A CMC is listed for 22-23 January 2026 to consider further disclosure, expert disciplines, testing of post-update
 characteristics and other such matters that are confirmed as issues for the CMC by the court.
 
The CMH2 judgment states at paragraph 124:

“The question of expert evidence is to be considered at the CMC in January 2026 and it is plainly the case that there is a fundamental dispute as to whether there should
 be the expert evidence currently contemplated. In particular, the unusual specialism of consumer behaviour is challenged and we were not entirely clear from the explanations of counsel as to the utility of such evidence.  Since the extent of the expert evidence
 still needs to be determined, we think it would be better to budget that phase once the court has ruled further.”

Paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment concludes:



“We propose to re-consider the budgeting of this phase in January alongside the expert reports phase in the Tranche
 3 budgets.”



The Defendants’ draft wording in the costs consequences order (not yet sealed), which we did not amend, currently
 states at paragraph 3:



“At the CMC listed in January 2026, the Court will consider whether there should be costs budgeting of the Expert
 Report phase of the parties’ Tranche 3 Budgets and/or the ADR phase of the parties’ Second General Budgets and, if so, give directions in that regard.”



The proposed draft wording departs from the judgment. The judgment proceeds on the basis that those phases
will be reconsidered for budgeting, whereas the draft order suggests only that the Court will consider whether there should be budgeting. What is clear is that budgeting for those phases (and potential "new" phases per the below) must occur, it
 is a question of when. 


Our proposal
We propose to write to the Defendants inviting amendment of paragraph 3 of the draft Order to reflect the judgment, namely,
 that the Court will reconsider budgeting of (i) the Expert Reports phases in Tranche 3 cost budgets; and (ii) the ADR phases in the Second General budgets. Further cost management directions will be provided at the January CMC. Although
 it would be advantageous to delay CMH3 if costs were to be deemed incurred until CMH3 (see option 2 below),  we believe that the best time for a potential CMH3 will be in February 2026. Any time after this will mean that a budgeting exercise is significantly
 less effective given a) March will not be a suitable time for this hearing to be listed as a result of the PDD Spring 2026 hearing which is listed for 3 weeks (a fourth in reserve) from 2 March 2026), and b) the phases that will be being considered in the
 cost budgeting will commence following the CMC in January and the costs of those phases will largely have been incurred before April 2026. We do, however, have a CMC listed in April 2026.  

Attendance at the January CMC
The question is whether attendance by costs counsel will be required at the January 2026 CMC. This will depend
 on whether further cost management directions can be agreed between the parties prior to the hearing. In any event, could you please confirm your availability for 22-23 January 2026, just in case.
 
Budgeting framework and incurred costs
As the Tranche 3 and Second General cost budgets have already been cost-managed, it may be considered that the T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases now fall within
 the PD3E §7.6 regime (variation to budgets).

We need to address how to present the T3 Expert Reports costs incurred between 17 July 2025 (the first day post-CMH2)
 and the listing of CMH3. There will be no incurred costs for the Second General ADR phase as it is not due to commence until 1 April 2026.


We suggest that the Lead Solicitors quantify those incurred costs in any event, but that:


·                    
Option 1: the “incurred to” date within the Cost Management Order remains 16 July 2025, with a note that £X has been incurred since that date and will form part of the
estimated allowance; or


·                    
Option 2: a separate cut-off date (CMH3) is adopted for the T3 Expert Reports phase only.


Preparation for budgeting


T3 Expert Reports Phase


There will be an initial change to the estimated costs within the T3 Expert Reports phase following the January
 CMC:


·                    
Scenario A: including consumer-behaviour expert evidence (if permission is granted at the January CMC), i.e. the version presented at CMH2; and
·                    
Scenario B: excluding those costs (if permission is not granted).

Scenario C: revising consumer- expert evidence costs (if the Court confirms that permission remains for the consumer-behaviour
 expert but clarifies/limits the scope)


However, the potential impact on the T3 Expert Reports phase extends beyond the consumer-behaviour expert application.
 If permission is refused, it may still impact the scope of the remaining expert evidence and the division of work among those experts.

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL

Dear all,

I hope you are all well. I write further to my last update on 5 August 2025, to provide you with a brief update on the following matters as they relate to the Ford NOx Emissions Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally
 (the “Litigation”):


PDD Trial Preparation;
Claimants Mechanical Expert;
Quantum Trial and discontinuance;
Change in personnel.

PDD Trial Preparation and final Pre-Trial Review

We are fast approaching the commencement of the PDD Trial, with the first day of trial listed for 13 October 2025, and the trial due to run until 19 December 2025.

Our skeleton argument was filed and served on 19 September, representing a mammoth undertaking by the entire Solicitor team and the barristers. The Ford specific annex to the skeleton argument was filed and served on 24 September. There was a slight extension
 to the Ford annex on account of the Defendants providing a very late second witness statement from a Ford employee. While we were not obliged to permit this into evidence, we took the view after considering it, that the statement was in fact more helpful for
 us and the case to allow its entry, rather than refusing permissions. As a caveat to our permittance of its inclusion, we agreed a short extension to the Ford annex.

As soon as I am in a position to provide you with a copy of the skeleton argument (with redactions for confidential information) I will send this to you. I would hope this will be later this week. I am extremely pleased with the final version of the skeleton
 argument. Our counsel team have done a remarkable job and it presents the best possible case for the court to consider.

While negotiations on the final timetable continue between the parties, we are close to concluding the timetable.

The first week of trial, due to commence on 13 October 2025, will consist of the Claimants and the Defendants making their opening remarks to the Court, in essence setting the scene, before we then move into evidence on what constitutes Normal Driving Conditions
 and then turning to each individual manufacturer. The order of the manufacturers will be Mercedes, Ford, Peugeot Citroen, Renault and Nissan.

It is expected that the Ford evidence, including the cross examination of experts and witnesses, will start on or around 13 November and run for just over a week.

If any of you are interested in attending Court for any part of the trial, please let us know and we will be able to arrange this with you.

There is due to be a final “Pre-Trial Review” hearing before the Court on 6 October which we are preparing for and this hearing will aim to settle any final issues or disputes that may impact the smooth running of the trial. The parties are in the process of
 agreeing an agenda for this hearing, and we will provide you with a further update on this in due course.

Claimants’ Software and Mechanical Experts

As per my previous update, I confirmed that in a hearing on 10 September, the Court unfortunately did not side with the Claimants in respect of the expert applications, and gave some strict directions with regard to steps the parties were required to take in
 respect of the software evidence that had been prepared.

We have been working hard to prepare and finalise the software report with the redactions / removals as advised by the Court and a version of these amended reports was provided to the Defendants on 24 September. We are awaiting the Defendants’ response to this
 draft report.  

In respect of the Claimants' mechanical expert, the Claimants' barrister team have provided a note to us in which they have flagged certain concerns with the mechanical expert. They have raised that they are concerned how the expert will perform at trial and
 that certain precautions need to be taken with the expert. Importantly, however, they have not told us that these concerns impact on the prospects of success of the case and we remain confident in the case we have prepared against Ford.

We are taking this note incredibly seriously and we are working hard, with the other Lead Solicitors, to prepare the expert for the trial. We are confident that, even with these concerns, the expert will be suitably prepared for trial, having undergone significant
 preparatory work before he takes the stand.

The expert is due to travel to the UK, from America, on 29 September, and will largely be based here, with the team, until his evidence is complete. He will observe various cross-examinations of other experts and will get a good feel for the experience he is
 likely to have in the witness box.

The team will also be assisting him in his preparation.

If you have any questions regarding this, please do let me and the Ford team know.

Quantum Trial

As you are aware, the Court has ordered that a second trial be listed in these NOx Litigations for October 2026. This trial, referred to as the “Quantum Trial” is in relation to the value of certain claims that are being brought by the Claimants. The Court
 will assess what value should be attributed to different heads of loss claimed by the Claimants, each of which were sustained as a result of the Defendants’ conduct, and determine a value for each claim being brought.

The Quantum Trial is proceeding, at least initially, on the basis of assumptions that the vehicles had prohibited defeat devices in them. This is necessary because we will not have a judgment from the Court on the defeat devices until at some point in mid-2026
 (post the October 2025 trial), and it is impractical for the entire litigation to grind to a half while waiting for this judgment. As such, we will prepare evidence and submissions on what we have pleaded for the PDD Trial, and this will then be updated, in
 very short order, once we have that judgment.

It is obviously impractical for the Court to hear evidence and consider losses on an individual basis (to do so would defeat the purpose of a group litigation), and so how this trial will proceed is by way of Sample Claimants. These are Claimants, selected
 between the Claimants and Defendants, who represent a range of characteristics and different issues across the Claimant cohort such that findings by the Court can be applied to all claimants. The characteristics that the Claimants needed to represent were
 included in Annex 2 to the October 2024 CMC Order, a copy of which is attached again for ease.

The process of negotiating these Sample Claimants took some time but the parties have finally reach agreement. A total of 40 Sample Claimants have been negotiated between the Claimants and Defendants across the Pan-NOx Litigations, split as eight per manufacturer,
 and of those eight, four selected by the Claimants, and four by the Defendants. Details of the Ford Sample Claimants can be provided if required.

Over the course of the negotiations, the Defendants made various nominations that the Claimants wished to resist, for various reasons i.e. the Claimants did not wish to participate as Sample Claimants, or they wished to pursue their claim in a different jurisdiction.
 In circumstances where those Sample Claimant nominees did not wish to proceed, the Defendants have taken the position that they must have their claims removed from the English Litigation. We have some sympathy with this, especially where Claimants wish to
 pursue their claim in a different jurisdiction.

Kenneth Gormley is one such person. Mr Gormley is a Ford Claimant, was nominated by the Defendants as a Sample Claimant, however we have since identified he is bringing a claim in both the England & Wales jurisdiction as part of this claim, and also in a separate
 litigation in Scotland.

Mr Gormley cannot continue with both claims and he was required to pick which one he wanted to continue with and we have instructions from Mr Gormley that he wishes to pursue his claim as part of the Scottish proceedings. We therefore are required to prepare
 and serve a formal notice of discontinuance in respect of Mr Gormley’s claim in the English proceedings.

Pursuant to paragraphs 29 and 30 of the Ford Group Litigation Order, we are seeking your instructions to act on Mr Gormley’s instructions and discontinue his claim.

Before confirming these instructions, we must advise you of the effect of this discontinuance. While it will not adversely impact the litigation, indeed the Litigation is already proceeding past this, the discontinuance will necessarily result in the Defendants
 being entitled to incur costs in the Litigation, that will be recoverable by them in due course.

As an initial reassurance, these costs will not be due from you or from any of the Claimants, but they will instead be covered, should they need to be paid, by either the ATE provider who is providing cover for this Litigation, or by Mr Gormley himself.

The general rule, under the governing Civil Procedure Rules 38.6 is that where a Claimant discontinues all or part of their claim, the Defendant has an automatic right to the costs they have incurred in respect of their claim.

There will be two types of costs that the Defendants will be able to recover: common costs, and individual costs.

As explained in the Client Committee meeting post the first Cost Management Hearing, the individual costs will be costs solely in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim, and the common costs will be the apportioned share of the Defendants overall costs of this exercise
 in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim. Mr Gormley’s claim is one claim out of hundreds of thousands, and so while we remain unaware of the level of costs that have been incurred by the Defendants, we believe the overall amount of the common costs will be minimal.

These costs cannot be resolved until the conclusion of the case and so there is no immediate cost that will be required to be paid.

I am of course available to discuss any aspect of this with you before you confirm your instructions, but I wish to reassure you that this discontinuance will not result in you, or any of the other thousands of claimants in the Litigation, being out of pocket.

As a result, we respectfully seek your instructions to:


Proceed to discontinue Mr Gormley’s claim in England & Wales; and
Remove Mr Gormley from the Ford Group Register.

Please confirm by return that you are content for us to take these steps

Change of Personnel

As a final piece of information, it is with regret that I must inform you that I have made the difficult decision to resign from my role at Pogust Goodhead.

I am currently working my notice period, with my final day of employment with the firm still subject to negotiation. As soon as I know when my final day is, I will inform you of this. I appreciate you will need to know this information.

Please rest assured that even with me having made the decision to part from the firm, I will be, and I am, continuing to act in the best interests of the Claimant Committee, and the wider claimant cohort. I personally have devoted a significant amount of time
 to this case and I am determined to ensure that the case is as best presented at trial as it can be.

I must also, at this point, advise you that the Partner with overall conduct of the Pan-NOx Litigations for Pogust Goodhead, Peter Gallagher, has also resigned. I am unable to comment on the reasons for his departure, but he has formally left the firm and the
 firm is putting in place a new head of the NOx department. They will contact you to confirm who this person is in due course. 

The remainder of the Ford Pogust Goodhead team remains in situ and they will continue to liaise with you. I remain with conduct of the matter, and when a decision has been made as to who will take conduct of the matter once I have departed, I will arrange for
 a handover to take place such that you are introduced to the new case lead.

Should you have any questions regarding the contents of this letter, please do not hesitate to contact us.

As always, we are grateful for your continued support and attention to the matter.

Yours faithfully,

Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Dear all,

I hope you are all well. I write further to my last update on 29 June 2025, to provide you with an update on the Ford NOx Emissions Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally (the “Litigation”)

As always, please note that the contents and existence of this letter are strictly privileged and confidential and should not be discussed with anyone other than us, as your legal representative, or other members of the Ford Claimant Committee.




In my previous update, I confirmed that we were set for an exceptionally busy July, with three hearings listed (De-designation, Cost Management and a Pre-Trial Review), in addition to the exchange of expert reports. I am pleased to say that we have successfully
 navigated each of those hearings, and exchanged our expert reports, and I set out below a full update in respect of each of those items. 




De-designation Hearing (“DDH”)



This DDH took place from 7 - 9 July before Mr Justice Constable and I am pleased to announce that it was a success for the Claimants. The judgment following the hearing was released on 25 July 2025 and can be found here:

https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Various-Claimants-v-Mercedes-Benz-Ford-Nissan-Stellantis-and-others.pdf




You can also find a helpful summary of the judgment here along with commentary from Pogust Goodhead and Leigh Day:

https://pogustgoodhead.com/dieselgate-high-court-blocks-attempts-by-car-manufacturers-to-hide-key-documents-that-could-show-whether-they-cheated-emissions-tests/




In short, the Court ruled that the Manufacturer Defendants cannot hide behind the cloak of confidentiality and must reveal hundreds of documents, including the parameters that the vehicles operate within, to the public. The Claimants were entirely justified
 in their application to lift confidentiality from these documents and the hearing will now be conducted in open court and subject to little or no reporting restrictions. There are still some documents that will retain their confidentiality, but it is a small
 number in comparison to the overall number of documents in the litigations. 




This is a significant victory in these cases, including in the Ford case, as it now means the Defendants must now reveal to the world how they calibrate and operate their vehicles. It also means that justice will be done publicly and without restriction - something
 the Defendants fought very hard to maintain. It further increases scrutiny on the Defendants from regulators and other public bodies to ensure that they are more closely examined and held to standard.




We are presently working on assembling all relevant documents that have previously been provided to you in redacted form, such as the Individual Particulars of Claim and we will update the SharePoint accordingly with those unredacted documents. 




Cost Management Hearing (“CMH”)




The CMH took place on 15 and 16 July before Mrs Justice Cockerill. The judgment following this hearing has not yet been handed down but we are expecting it to be over the course of the summer break and hopefully before September. We will update you as soon
 as we know more regarding this.




Pre-Trial Review (“PTR”)




The PTR took place on 28 and 29 July, again before Mrs Justice Cockerill. The Court gave guidance on a number of procedural issues including the expected timetable for Trial i.e. what order the cases will be heard in and how long each case will be heard in
 court, the Trial bundle of documents and protocols governing how the parties are to interact in advance of the hearing. None of this involves any work that you as the Claimants need to undertake. 




What is of significance however are the two applications that we made to be heard at the PTR in respect of Ford. As forecast in my previous update, we did ultimately make an application for Specific Disclosure of certain additional relevant information from
 Ford. Following sustained negotiations with the Defendants in respect of this, the parties have been able to reach an agreement on certain specific further documentation that Ford are to provide us with by 15 August 2025. 




Secondly, and importantly, we submitted an application for permission to amend our pleadings. The need for this arose following our review of documents that we had received from the Defendants which indicated that there is a defect in certain of the Defendant
 Vehicles which in turn affects the PDDs that we allege are in the vehicles. Ford are nervous about this information and they sought to oppose this amendment to the pleadings. The Court opted to not deal with the application at the PTR but instead to deal with
 it at a hearing in future, potentially in September.




This amendment and bringing the defect to light and into the public will have a significantly positive impact on the case as it bring a host of new pleadings against the Defendants. 




We will keep you updated on the progress of this application.




The other key point the Court dealt with was in relation to expert evidence at the PTR. The Defendants, most notably Ford, have been making a series of on-going complaints regarding the contents of our expert reports, stating that they feel the reports go outside
 the remit of the experts. We of course aver that they do not, instead considering that the Defendants' complaints are instead a cover for their nervousness about their contents. Ford in particular have been raising issues regarding the software report that
 we have filed, primarily we believe because our expert has done an excellent job and presented a very damaging case to Ford that increases the prospects of success at trial. 




The Court has advised that a further hearing on 10 September will be listed to hear any arguments over the contents of the expert reports, with the parties to try and resolve the issues prior to the date of the hearing. We will keep you informed as to this. 




Ford Litigation specific matters




Expert Reports




Per the below update, the initial expert reports have now been exchanged (on the 25 and 27 July respectively) and we are moving towards the third step previously advised: the exchange of supplemental expert reports. This is due to occur on the 22nd August. 




Our initial review of the expert reports provided by the Defendants is that they do not contain any surprises or give us real cause for concern. Their software report is considerably less in-depth than ours, to our advantage, while their mechanical engineer
 also appears to have struggled to formulate a strong case in Ford's favour. 




Claimant Committee Members




We are continuing to engage with Virgin Media over their appointment to the Committee and there is no substantive update on this at this point. 




Should any of you have any further questions arising out of this update, please do not hesitate to get in contact with me to discuss.

As always, please note that the contents and existence of this letter are strictly privileged and confidential and should not be discussed with anyone other than us, as your legal representative, or other members of the Ford Claimant Committee.

Having previously updated you on the March and May CMCs, I am pleased to inform you that we have now agreed the resultant Orders from those hearings and copies of these are attached.

As you will discern, those Orders do update previous directions, especially the May Order which now sets out a more detailed process for disclosure in respect of the Quantum Trial in October 2026,  Details of these updates were contained in my previous update.

As detailed below, the team is currently preparing for a very busy July including three substantive hearings across the month: the de-designation hearing, which is listed between 7 - 9 July 2025; a Cost Management Hearing in respect of the Quantum Trial, which
 is listed between 14 – 16 July 2025; and finally the Pre-Trial Review (the “PTR”) which is listed on 28 and 29 July.

We are also preparing our final expert reports which are due to be exchanged on 16 July 2025, while supplementary reports are to be exchanged on 30 July.

In light of the exceptionally busy July, I may be unable to provide you with a substantive update until August, but I will endeavour to provide you with any relevant updates following the hearings as required.

Below I set out an update in respect of those three substantive hearings and a general update on the Ford Litigation.

De-designation Hearing (“DDH”)

One key hurdle the parties face in these Pan-NOx Litigations is that there are significant barriers erected between the Litigations that prevent the efficient and effective exchange and comparison of information and disclosure between the cases. This is a fundamental
 part of the Claimants claim i.e. that many of the manufacturers were either sharing strategies and technology to insert prohibits defeat devices (“PDDs”) in their vehicles, or alternatively, that better technology was available that was being used by
 other manufacturers that mean the Defendants did not need to insert PDDs in their vehicles.

As mentioned in previous updates, much the information that exists in the Ford Litigation, and similarly in the other Lead Cases (Mercedes, Renault/Nissan and Peugeot Citroën) is subject to a case specific Confidentiality Ring Orders (“CRO”). Each of
 the Lead cases has their own CRO. The Defendants have taken this CRO as a means to try and keep secret the majority of the documentation that they have provided to us, thereby restricting access to the documents to persons who are members of the CRO. Despite
 protestations from the Defendants, we have successfully implemented a Pan-Lead CRO, which has been constructed to assist in the sharing of confidential information across the cases. While this is helpful in permitted us to see documents from other cases, it
 does not alleviate the issue of transferring documents into the Pan-Lead CRO (as the Defendants continue to raise various issues regarding this) and it does not prevent those documents being confidential and only certain people being able to see them. This
 does not go to the principle of open justice, whereby the public should know the conduct of these manufacturers. It is and always has been our intention to seek to de-designate these documents so that they can be referred to openly and in public.

The DDH is shaped at doing precisely that; bringing those documents into the public and also to make the process of hearing these cases in court more feasible. Under present circumstances, any time a party wishes to discuss any documentation that is confidential,
 it would require the Court room to be emptied of people who are not within the CROs, which is simply unworkable. The DDH is intended to allow open justice to be carried out. 

The Claimants prepared and filed their respective applications and witness evidence on 13 June 2025 and we took receipt of the Defendants’ responsive evidence late last night. We are considering this with our counsel team in advance of the preparation of skeleton
 arguments and the hearing itself.

Cost Management Hearing (“CMH”)

A Cost Management Hearing is scheduled for 14-16 July 2025. The purpose of this hearing is for the parties to agree the costs budgets in relation to the Quantum Trial, which is set to take place in October 2026.

You may recall we undertook a similar exercise last July in respect of costs for the PDD Trial, which we are hurtling towards in October of this year.

We have instructed the same counsel team as represented us last year which has assisted us in considering the rulings of the Court at that hearing. Our budgets were exchanged with the Defendants on 17 June and we have been considering them since. We are due
 to provide a response to the Defendants budgets in documents knows as Budget Discussion Report (“BDRs”) on 3 July and we are working with our counsel team to prepare these now. We image the BDRs may assist in bring about more agreement with the Defendants
 and in advance of skeleton arguments which are due on 10 July 2025.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.

Pre-Trial Review (“PTR”)

The final hearing in July and before the summer break is the PTR. Generally this hearing is reserved for procedural matters, including timetabling for the main trial, the running order of issues and the trial bundle, as opposed to any more substantive issues
 between the parties.

However, in these cases which are extraordinary, it is likely that this PTR will deal with a larger number of issues including any final applications that the Claimants may wish to make before the Court takes its summer vacation. In the Ford Litigation, we
 are consider submitting applications for specific documents however we have not yet arrived at the final decision on that point.  

Preparation for this hearing has already commenced and the teams are identifying issues that they may require to be resolved at that hearing.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.




Ford Litigation specific matters

Without Prejudice Meeting – HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL

A preliminary confidential meeting with Ford took place on 12 June 2025 to discuss the merits of the case. As mentioned in our previous update, the aim of this meeting was to inform the Ford Defendants of the strength of our case and seek to narrow the issues
 between the parties.

In attendance at the meeting were our the Claimant and Defendant counsel teams, as well as some of the Solicitors and Ford also sent one of their internal general counsel to attend. During the meeting, the barristers presented a number of key confidential documents
 to Fords legal team and ventilated a number of high level issues about the case, many of which the Ford became defensive about. While the meeting has not yielded any immediate results, from the Claimants' perspective it was positive and we viewed the meeting
 as having done what it needed to.

We have not yet heard anything further from Ford (which was expected) but we will keep you updated if and when we hear anything further from them.

Claimant Committee Members

With your previous consent, we have officially appointed Keith Turner as a new Claimant Committee Member. We are awaiting a signed copy of the Claimant Committee Agreement from Virgin Media before they are appointed as a member, and once that is concluded,
 we will confirm the new Claimant Committee and convene a meeting.

This will likely take place in August. 

Testing

As mentioned in our previous update, the parties have been undergoing tests on all 6 Sample Vehicles. These tests are now concluded, and, as expected, the results in many instances have proven to be excellent in assisting the case we are advancing. The results
 of the testing have been provided to both the Claimant and Defendant experts who are analysing them to incorporate into their reports.

Expert Reports

A crucial step in preparing our case for trial. Our experts (in the fields of automotive software and mechanical engineering) are currently preparing reports outlining their analysis of the test results and their findings and opinion regarding PDDs that are
 contained in Ford vehicles.

This is a 3 step process, the first step having already been concluded.


A meeting(s) between the experts to formulate a Joint Statement which sets out where the experts opinions align. This has been completed and a copy of the report has been added to the SharePoint.
Exchange of main Expert reports exchanged between the parties . These reports are compiled independent from the other side and represent the individual exerts opinions and findings based upon the test results and disclosure. Our experts are working hard to
 finalise their reports and we are meeting with them regularly to assist them in any way we can.
Exchange of Supplementary Expert Reports. Once the reports at step 2 above are exchanged, the experts have time to consider the content of those reports and then update any opinions in their own report based on what the other expert has said. Work on this will
 commence immediately after exchange of the reports.

Disclosure and Witness Evidence

As foreshadowed in the previous update, all tranches of disclosure have now been received from the Defendants and a mass review exercise is on-going. To date, the Ford Defendants have disclosed approximately 38,000 documents that the combined teams of Pogust
 Goodhead and Leigh Day are reviewing these to assist in substantiating our case. Some documents include evidence from the Defendants showing they had updates available for the vehicles, as they knew they were problematic, however they deigned not to implement
 them at the time for internal reasons, and other documents show that Ford opted for different strategies in their vehicles in comparison to others due to cost considerations.

All of this information is incredibly helpful both for our counsel team who will be presenting the information in court but also for our team of experts who will be considering disclosure as part of their report.

We have also taken receipt of a Witness Statement served by Ford from one of their employees who was involved in the development of the their diesel engines. They have served this in an effort to rebut our case, however the statement is quite helpful in a number
 of ways, including alluding to documents which may be damaging to Ford’s case. We and our counsel team are continuing to analyse this, and we are engaging with Ford on the document and its contents. It is thought that this individual will attend the trial
 and he will be cross-examined by our counsel team.

Group Register and Notices of Objection

The official deadline for service of the sixth iteration of the Group Register was on Friday, 20 June 2025.While the Group Register, per the terms of the GLO, is due to be served every three months, In light, of the other competing deadlines in the upcoming
 months, we have agreed with the Defendants to an extension of this deadline to 20 September 2025. We are reviewing our Group Register data ahead of the next iteration and will keep you updated.

The Defendants have also provided further objections regarding a small number of claims enrolled in the fourth iteration of the Group Register. As they are only able to raise objections in respect of “new” claims enrolled on the Group Register,  or existing

Further to our discussion last week, please review the sheet “Mercedes, Pan NOx, L&A Costs” within the attached spreadsheet (link:

 Mercedes, Pan, L&A Common Cost Schedules.xlsx​​)

Sophia, Jamie and I have prepared three tables:



Schedule 1: Mercedes-only common costs

Schedule 2: All Pan-NOx common costs

Schedule 3: All Lead & ALGLO combined common costs


Total common costs claimed
Each table is divided into the relevant cost budgets, displaying incurred costs (column D) and approved costs (column F) from the First Costs Management Hearing (CMH1) and the Second Costs Management Hearing (CMH2). These figures mirror exactly what
 the Court ordered and what the Defendants will be expecting.

We have also included “Non-Budgeted” cost rows (11, 24, 37), with explanations (column L). These reflect incurred costs of which the Defendants are only partially aware due to interim Statements of Costs etc.

Recovery against common costs claimed
We have applied a 60% recovery rate on all incurred costs (column E). This figure can be adjusted, and the tables will self-calculate.

We have also added adjustments to the approved budgeted costs (column G) to show the pro-rata budgeted amounts we can expect to recover, with explanations (column J).

Liability apportionment on recovered costs
The schedule summary then applies the proposed proportionate share method of apportionment for Mercedes:


100% of Mercedes-only common costs (row 42)

23.68% of Pan-NOx costs (row 43)

44.77% of Lead & ALGLO costs (row 44)


Total common cost settlement
All interim costs awards have then been credited (G46), with details of payment made outlined in the table “Interim Costs Orders Paid.” 

We then divided the adjusted total common cost settlement figure (G67) by the number of claims in the Mercedes Group Register as of 1st October 2025 (428,371) to obtain the total common cost settlement per claim (G68).

Next steps
We expect a call may be the best way to go through the schedule in detail, but in the meantime, two points to consider are:



Non-budgeted costs:
It is difficult to obtain a complete picture of non-budgeted common costs, and these are, in any event, particularly hard to recover inter partes.
Where we have costs orders in our favour, supported by Statements of Costs but without any interim payment, these are itemised in the “Interim Costs Orders Unpaid” table. This total forms part of the Mercedes specific non-budgeted costs.
However, PG/LD/MiB alone still have a further £762,402.17 of non-budgeted WIP outside of these Statements. I suspect this relates largely to ATE/AAE/SfC funding issues and disbursement reconciliation, all of which will be tenuous in terms of recovery.
We also do not yet know the total of any non-PG/LD/MiB firms’ non-budgeted common costs.
We may need to decide whether to (a) limit non-budgeted costs to the amounts the Defendants are aware of, or (b) include all our non-budgeted totals in the model but use the non-budgeted costs as a concession as part of the negotiations. 

Apportionment:
Which Pan-NOx / Lead & ALGLO apportionment method do we want to adopt? All three options are included in the sheet “Pan NOx, L&A Apportionment” for discussion. We have applied Option 2, the Proportionate Share method, within the table.


Best,
Sarah
